name: THS7374IPWR
title: Four-channel SDTV video amplifier with sixth-order filters and 6 dB gain
summary: A four-channel video buffer for standard-definition signals that runs from a single 3 V to 5 V supply. Each channel has a fixed gain of 2 V/V (6 dB), a sixth-order Butterworth low-pass filter with a 9.5 MHz corner that can be bypassed for 150 MHz bandwidth, and an input that works dc-coupled with a 150 mV level shift, ac-coupled with a sync-tip clamp, or ac-coupled with an external bias resistor. The rail-to-rail outputs drive one or two 75 Ω video lines, dc- or ac-coupled. Quiescent current is 9.6 mA at 3.3 V and a disable pin drops it to 0.1 µA. It comes in a 14-pin TSSOP.
key_figures: 6th-order Butterworth, 9.5 MHz (–3 dB), 8.2 MHz (–1 dB), 54 dB at 27 MHz

circuits.title: 3.3-V single-supply, dc-input/dc-output coupled video line driver
circuits.description: A 3.3 V SDTV DAC or encoder feeds all four inputs directly; each DAC output carries its own termination resistor R to ground, sized for the DAC. CH1 takes composite video and CH2 to CH4 take Y'/G', P'B/B' and P'R/R'. Every output drives its line straight, through a 75 Ω source resistor, into a 75 Ω termination at the receiving end. DISABLE and BYPASS go to a GPIO controller or to ground, and VS+ runs from +3 V to +5 V.

circuits.title: Low-cost SCART switching system
circuits.description: A video SOC/DAC drives R', G' and B' into CH2 to CH4; its CVBS/Sync output and the VCR SCART's CVBS input meet at one section of a CD4053 switch whose common feeds CH1. CH1 drives the composite outputs of both SCART connectors and CH2 to CH4 drive the TV SCART's R', G' and B' pins, each through 75 Ω and an optional 330 µF capacitor. Two more CD4053 sections pick the TV audio from either the SOC amplifiers or the VCR SCART audio inputs, which are biased through 100 kΩ resistors from +VBIAS. The VCR SCART's pin 8 sets the switch through 220 Ω with 22 kΩ to ground. Two transistors driven from GPIO set the TV SCART's pin 8 level for standby and aspect ratio, and a GPIO drives the fast-blanking line through 75 Ω.

operation.text: Each of the four channels has an input with an 800 kΩ resistor to ground and a sync-tip clamp, a level shift, a six-pole 9.5 MHz low-pass filter that BYPASS can switch out, and an output amplifier with 6 dB of gain. The part is built on a complementary SiGe BiCom3X process.

The part runs from 3 V to 5 V over –40 °C to +85 °C; thin-film resistors and low-temperature-coefficient capacitors keep performance almost constant with temperature. It works down to 2.85 V, but at least 3 V is advised to keep headroom. Quiescent current totals 9.6 mA at 3.3 V and 10 mA at 5 V.

A 0.1 µF to 0.01 µF capacitor goes as close to the supply pin as possible, or the outputs may ring or oscillate. A larger capacitor, 22 µF to 100 µF, on the supply line reduces 50 Hz/60 Hz interference.

A high level on DISABLE shuts the part down to about 0.1 µA; its outputs then look like 20 kΩ in parallel with 3 pF. A high level on BYPASS routes the signal around the filters, giving 150 MHz bandwidth and 130 V/µs slew rate. Disable and enable take about 100 ns at 3.3 V and 80 ns at 5 V; switching between filter and bypass takes 5 ns. Neither pin may be left floating.
The input accepts about –0.2 V to VS+ – 1.5 V, but with the 2 V/V gain and the 150 mV shift the output limits the linear range first: on 5 V the linear input is about –0.1 V to 2.3 V.

Every input and output pin has ESD diodes to both supply rails. The internal breakdown voltages are low, as the absolute maximum ratings show. The diodes give moderate protection against overdrive beyond the rails and can typically carry 30 mA continuously.

Many DACs and encoders connect directly. The input sees only the internal 800 kΩ to ground; the level shift appears at the output, not at the input pin. A 0 V input adds 150 mV inside and, after the 6 dB gain, gives about 300 mV at the output, keeping the bottom of sync clear of the output's lower limit so that no sync is clipped. The shift is the same for every input level.

For sources referenced to the positive supply, a series capacitor (nominally 0.1 µF) feeds the input and an internal loop holds the lowest input level at 0 V. The clamp is an active dc-restore loop, not a diode, and does nothing while the input stays above ground, so a dc-coupled input also works. When the input dips below 0 V the loop sources current in proportion, up to 3 mA, then turns to high impedance once the level is back above 0 V. A low-pass filter in the loop delays its response by roughly 800 ns so it clamps on the flat sync tip rather than on overshoot; the loop depends only on the instantaneous input voltage, not on timing.

The 800 kΩ to ground supplies the discharge current that pulls an ac-coupled level down toward the clamp; small current means little line tilt but slower sync capture (hum rejection). Cutting the coupling capacitor from 0.1 µF to 0.047 µF doubles hum rejection; an extra external pull-down raises the discharge current. A 10 pF to 47 pF capacitor to ground beside the input termination resistors helps filter overshoot.

With the input capacitor fitted the source impedance must be below 1 kΩ or the clamp loop may ring and show at the output. DAC terminations are usually under 300 Ω; with a high-impedance source, a 1 kΩ resistor to ground solves it.

For signals without sync (C', P'B, P'R, U', V', R'G'B' without sync) a pull-up resistor to the supply sets the dc level after the coupling capacitor. The output bias should sit between 0.9 V and VS+ – 1 V; 100 % saturated CVBS or Macrovision signals reach 1.23 VPP at the input (2.46 VPP at the output), other signals about 0.7 VPP (1.4 VPP). The bias follows the supply, which costs PSRR; the input capacitor and pull-up form a low-pass filter that reduces this and also set the settling time. The sync-tip clamp keeps a steadier back porch than ac bias does.

The rail-to-rail output drives the line directly, avoiding large capacitors and giving the best line and field tilt; tilt from an ac-coupled input still reaches the output. The output drives 80 mA, enough for two lines (a 75 Ω load). An ac-biased output into ground-terminated lines draws dc current, lowering the high swing and adding under 10 mW per channel. Each line needs a 75 Ω series termination placed close to the output pin to isolate capacitive load; stray capacitance on the output pin must stay under 20 pF, and any output capacitor goes after the resistor.

A coupling capacitor of 220 µF to 1000 µF (470 µF is common) in series with the 75 Ω source resistor keeps line and field tilt low and lets the receiver set its own dc level. Each of two lines should have its own resistor and capacitor; sharing one 1000 µF capacitor risks ground loops and interference between receivers. A 0.1 µF to 0.01 µF capacitor across the electrolytic is optional and lowers impedance above 1 MHz. Chroma lines in S-video can use smaller capacitors, such as 0.1 µF.

Each channel has a sixth-order Butterworth filter with a 9.5 MHz –3 dB corner and a –1 dB passband of 8.2 MHz, for SD NTSC, PAL and SECAM CVBS, S-video, 480i/576i Y'P'BP'R, Y'U'V', G'B'R' and computer video. Attenuation is 54 dB at 27 MHz, 60 dB at 54 MHz, 55 dB at 81 MHz, 50 dB at 108 MHz and at least 45 dB above 108 MHz. The corner allows for process spread; temperature effects are held down by low-tempco resistors and capacitors, which also keep channel-to-channel delay low.

The input is 800 kΩ with 2 pF plus board capacitance, so the DAC's voltage is set by a fixed termination resistor. The output behaves as a low-impedance voltage source, about 0.7 Ω at 5 MHz, so a 75 Ω series resistor matches the line.

The EVM has BNC connectors, 75 Ω input terminations, 75 Ω series output resistors and 75 Ω traces, and runs from a single 2.85 V to 5 V supply. By default the inputs are dc-coupled, needing a signal within 0 V to about 1.4 V, and the outputs are ac-coupled with 470 µF and 0.1 µF.
